en: A Single Section from the *Buddhabhāṣita-vajramaṇḍala-vyūha-prajñāpāramitā-nirdeśa*,
a Branch Circulation from the Great Collection;
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Translated by the Dharma Master Śīladharma, recipient of the purple robe and subject of the Emperor. At that time, all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions again gathered like clouds and entreated:
“World-Honored One, Vajrayoga Great Secret Lord, Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, we pray that you will expound the Dharma-gate of the Fundamental Non-substantiality Prajñāpāramitā.”

At that time, the World-Honored One, Vajrayoga-Mahāguhyapati Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, having heard the exhortations of all the Tathāgatas, immediately entered the Great Wisdom-Vajra Samādhi of the Realm of All Buddhas. Emerging from this samādhi, in a single kṣaṇa, he abided within the nature of the vajra-reality wisdom of all the Tathāgatas and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
Within this nature, he further entered the samādhi of the wisdom of the wondrous, firm, and solid nature of the heart-light of all Tathāgatas.

Within this samādhi, from the hearts of all Tathāgatas, there emerged the light of the realm of all Buddhas, which universally illumined the entire Dharma-realm, reaching everywhere and shining throughout the entire realm of sentient beings, causing the wisdom of all sentient beings to become pure.

From the bodhicitta of all sentient beings, the empowerment method for the hook-summoning of reverence and love is born; it is perfectly accomplished through the vajrasattva samādhi, established according to principle as it was well-performed.
Furthermore, from the Great Being Ratnārci-ketu-hasita-guhya, there arises the nature of supreme Maheśvara, abiding within the awakening-nature of the Vajrasattva-samādhi.

Furthermore, from the Great Being of the Secret Speech, which is the cause of the benefits of the Dharma, there arises the purity of the actions performed by the firm mind; abiding in the self-nature purity of the supreme *dharmatā*-treasury of the Lotus-Sattva Samādhi, one establishes various superior activities from this state to protect and care for the Dharma and bring sentient beings to maturity.

Having brought all sentient beings within the realm of existence to full maturity and established them in their proper state through the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, he returned once more to the heart of the Bhagavān Mahāvairocana Tathāgata and dwelt, entering into the nature of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, spoke these verses:
"How great is the stainless cause of right wisdom, From which all Tathāgatas are born!
Right wisdom is immaculate and inconceivable, The source from which the nature of the multitudes of sentient beings arises."
How great are all phenomena, inconceivable! All buddha-deeds are utterly pure;
yet when one discriminates between existence and non-existence, this mind revolves within these two extremes.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī manifested supernatural powers within the assembly; from the heart of the Tathāgata, he emanated the bodies of sixteen great Bodhisattvas who surrounded the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana. To the left and right of all the Tathāgatas, he manifested the radiance of the Mahāvairocana Maṇḍala, and within that light, he further manifested the Maṇḍala of the Sublime Moon.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī sat in the center and spoke these words:
“I entreat the World-Honored One, Vajrayoga-Mahāguhyapati Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, to proclaim the various true Dharma verses of the *Vajramaṇḍalavyūha-prajñāpāramitā* teachings.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
Mañjuśrī! You are able to ask the Buddha about such a correct principle.
Listen attentively and apply your mind well; I shall now proclaim it for you.

At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, abiding in the sovereign nature of all Tathāgatas, spoke the great mantra-words of the Prajñāpāramitā of the Array of the Vajra-maṇḍala, namely the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth.
"The four foundations of mindfulness consist of: observing with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension the body within, the body without, and the body both within and without;
observing with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension feelings within, feelings without, and feelings both within and without;
and observing with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension the mind within, the mind without, and the mind both within and without."
Regarding phenomena, whether internal or external, one observes them with right mindfulness and right awareness.

Thus, through the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness—body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—if one possesses right mindfulness and right awareness, then all is pure, one abides in non-attachment, and there is ultimately nothing whatsoever in the world; yet body, speech, and mind constantly abide in the gate of the Dharma of equality, the Prajñāpāramitā. This is called the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā on the equality of the four foundations of mindfulness.
The Great Illumination says:

“‘Aṃ (prolonged) 1; Gaṃ (prolonged) 2; Oṃ caṭṭāri samitī tadyathā praseṭhānāṃ 3. Furthermore, regarding the four right efforts: it means that for unwholesome states not yet arisen, one arouses diligence so that they shall not arise, and collects the mind with right mindfulness;
for unwholesome states already arisen, one arouses diligence so that they may be completely abandoned, and collects the mind with right mindfulness.”
For all wholesome states that have not yet arisen, he arouses diligence so that they may all be brought forth and grow; he collects the mind in right mindfulness.

For all wholesome states that have already arisen, he arouses diligence so that they may all increase, becoming firm, vast, cultivated, perfected, and fully developed through the collection of the mind in right mindfulness.

These four right endeavors are the non-interruption of all phenomena while simultaneously being their interruption; this is the realization of the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya). This is called the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, the vast gateway of the right endeavors.

The Great Illumination says: "Oṃ samyakprahāṇa sarvatathāgatasamādhiṣṭhāya a ra hūṃ. Furthermore, there are the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*): the base of spiritual power consisting of the concentration of desire and the perfection of the exercise of abandonment; the base of spiritual power consisting of the concentration of diligence and the perfection of the exercise of abandonment; the base of spiritual power consisting of the concentration of mind and the perfection of the exercise of abandonment; and the base of spiritual power consisting of the concentration of wisdom and the perfection of the exercise of abandonment.

These four bases of miraculous power arise from the illusory nature of all phenomena; they are the gateway to the essence of the ultimate truth of the Prajñāpāramitā that turns the wheel of all dharmas. This is called the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā of the wisdom of equality regarding the perfection of the bases of miraculous power.
The Great Illumination says:

"Oṃ r̥ti-praṇāvara-mite lava-ya-ra hūṃ hūṃ. Furthermore, there are the five faculties (pañcendriya), namely: the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

When these five faculties thus operate within the equality of all phenomena, entirely free from conceptual proliferation, this is called the teaching on the Prajñāpāramitā of the Equality of the Faculties.
The Great Illumination says:

"Oṃ indriyavaśitāprabhāve jñānam ātmabhāvagatāya ā oṃ. Furthermore, there are the five powers, namely: the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of meditative concentration, and the power of wisdom.

These five powers are the equal practice of all dharmas; they are entirely free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding all powers and are primordially pure. This is called the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* on the Augmentation of Powers.
The Great Illumination says:

“Oṃ sarvatathāgatamālā āḥ hūṃ hūṃ vaḥ. Furthermore, there are the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga), namely: the factor of mindfulness, the factor of investigation of phenomena, the factor of diligence, the factor of joy, the factor of tranquility, the factor of concentration, and the factor of equanimity.
These seven dharmas abide in the nature of equality; this is called the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* characterized by the manifestation of equality.

The great mantra is: "Oṃ saptatrigasamata subratitiṣṭhe tvaṃ vaṃ. Furthermore, the Eightfold Noble Path consists of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right awareness.

These eight dharmas give rise to the inexhaustible right path from the great bodhicitta, and one thoroughly awakens to the knowledge of all modes; this is called the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā of the equality of the Eightfold Noble Path.
The Great Illumination says:
"Oṃ āryeṣṭāṅgamudrāsthita. Furthermore, there are three samādhis, namely: emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness (animitta), and wishlessness (apraṇihita).
What is called the samādhi of emptiness?

It refers to the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristic of non-existence, and the characteristic of lack of intrinsic nature; these are identical in their single characteristic with all phenomena. This characteristic is unborn; this is what is called the samādhi of emptiness.
What is called the signless samādhi?

It refers to when, regarding all phenomena, one is without the mark of volitional activity, without expectation, without differentiation, and abides in the mark of tranquility and the mark of detachment; with the mind stilled in a single object, this is called the signless samādhi.
What is called the *asaṃskāra-samādhi* (wishless concentration)?

It refers to the absence of cognitive apprehension and the absence of volitional activity regarding all phenomena—such as their characteristics of suffering, impermanence, and so forth. Whether one knows them in this way or otherwise, there is no seeking, no striving, and no aspiration; this is what is called the *asaṃskāra-samādhi*.
These three samādhis, and even all natures and all doors of samādhi, enter accordingly through the door of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Great Illumination says:
"Oṃ (1) kha-samā-sarva-dharma (2) khaṃ (3). Furthermore, there are the eight liberations: namely, the liberation of perceiving external forms while possessing internal form-perception;
the liberation of perceiving external forms while lacking internal form-perception;"
The liberation of purity;

furthermore, transcending all perceptions of form, not giving rise to perceptions of resistance, and not forming the notion of "self," one practices contemplation by taking infinite space as the object—this is the liberation of the sphere of infinite space;
furthermore, transcending the sphere of infinite space, one practices contemplation by taking infinite consciousness as the object—this is the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Furthermore, transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one practices contemplation by taking the sphere of nothingness as the object; this is the liberation of the sphere of nothingness.

Furthermore, transcending the sphere of nothingness, one practices contemplation by taking the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the object; this is the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one correctly practices contemplation within the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling.

These eight dharmas are the nature of all phenomena as free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*): they are neither defiled nor pure, neither concentrated nor distracted, neither *samāpatti* nor non-*samāpatti*. This is called the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* that transcends what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).
The Great Illumination says:

“Oṃ (1) samantavajri (2) sarvabāva-viśuddhe (3) taṃ (4) taṃ (5) kaṃ (6). Furthermore, there are the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*): namely, the first dhyāna-concentration, which is free from desires and all evil, unwholesome dharmas, and possesses applied and sustained thought, arising from seclusion and characterized by joy and bliss;

and the second dhyāna-concentration, wherein that applied and sustained thought has ceased, the internal mind is purified and remains in one-pointedness, being without applied or sustained thought, and arising from concentration with joy and bliss.
Being detached from joy, one dwells in equanimity and mindfulness, experiencing sublime bliss with the body; this is the third dhyāna, the state of sublime bliss free from joy.

When both the states of suffering and pleasure are entirely abandoned, and previous feelings of mental elation and distress have ceased, one experiences neither suffering nor pleasure; with equanimity and mindfulness purified, this is the fourth dhyāna.

Transcending all perceptions of form, not giving rise to perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one contemplates the sphere of infinite space; this is the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space.

Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one practices contemplation by taking infinite consciousness as the object; this is the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*).

Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one practices contemplation by taking the sphere of nothingness as the object; this is the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).

Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one practices contemplation by taking the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the object; this is the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*).

And the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling—these nine phenomena, whether they possess intrinsic nature or lack intrinsic nature, are all free from conceptual discrimination. This is the non-dual realization of the equality of all phenomena; it is called the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā of the Equality of All Liberations.
The Great Illumination says:

"Oṃ ānata-vimokṣa-mukha-saṃ [1]. Furthermore, there are the six recollections (ṣaḍ-anusmṛti), namely: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of renunciation, recollection of ethical discipline, and recollection of the devas.

Thus, these six dharmas and all phenomena are, in a single moment of thought, the ultimate emptiness; all phenomena share a single characteristic, namely signlessness, which is itself free from characteristics. This is called the samādhi of the gate of equality, and it is designated by the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Great Illumination says:

“Oṃ sarvānusaṃmiti vāraṃ taṃ saṃ padanideśi hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ. Furthermore, there are ten stages of a bodhisattva: the stage of generating the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*), the stage of youthful purity (*kumārabhūta*), the stage of initial practice (*ādikarmika*), the stage of cultivation (*prayoga*), the stage of noble birth (*janmakalyāṇa*), the stage of perfection of application (*pratisaṃyukta-paripūrṇa*), the stage of right mind (*samyakcitta*), the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), the stage of receiving empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), and the stage of being born with only one more life remaining (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

Thus, the stages of a bodhisattva are not actually stages; by transcending all stages, one enters the ultimate truth and abides in the nature of a single stage. This "single stage" is itself stageless; this is called the teaching of the stageless Prajñāpāramitā.
The Great Illumination says:

"Oṃ sarvameghasatnavigate hūṃ. Furthermore, there are the ten masteries of a bodhisattva, namely: mastery over lifespan, mastery over karma, mastery over requisites, mastery over resolute belief, mastery over vows, mastery over supernormal powers, mastery over birth, mastery over power, mastery over phenomena, and mastery over the mind.

These ten masteries are, in fact, not masteries, because their intrinsic nature is detached; thus one attains the most supreme tranquility among all masteries—the pure nature in which all phenomena are well-established. This is called the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā of All Masteries.
The Great Illumination says:

"Oṃ sarvavāśite traṃ truṃ hūṃ. Furthermore, there are the ten pāramitās, namely: the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of skillful means, the perfection of aspiration, the perfection of power, and the perfection of knowledge.

Thus, these ten *pāramitās* encompass all *pāramitās*: they are the *pāramitā* of the unequaled, the *pāramitā* free from conceptual proliferation, the *pāramitā* of the meaning as it truly is, the *pāramitā* of the true meaning of all phenomena, the *vajra-pāramitā*, the *ratna-pāramitā*, the *dharma-pāramitā*, the *karma-pāramitā*, and the *pāramitā* of the equality of all phenomena. All such dharmas abide within this firm, conforming, and corresponding gateway of the Dharma; this is called the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* that is equal to all *pāramitās*.
The Great Illumination states:

"Oṃ sarvaparāmitāparivartani oṃ praṃ hūṃ dhaṃ. Furthermore, there are the ten stages, namely: the Stage of Joy, the Stage of Purity, the Stage of Radiance, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage Difficult to Conquer, the Stage of Presence, the Stage of Far-Going, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Stage of the Dharma Cloud.
Thus, these ten stages are all stages that share a single meaning, namely, the meaning of wisdom (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, this very meaning of wisdom is non-existent; it is signless, without letters, without sound, and without name. It cannot be designated, is primordially pure, manifests stainless light, and abides in the true meaning. This is called the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* of the purity of the stages.
The Great Illumination says:

"Oṃ bhumivijayini sarvārthaparipūraṇi vaṃ paṃ. Furthermore, there are the four Brahma-vihāras, namely: loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā).
These four dharmas abide in the holy life; this is called the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā on the equality of all phenomena.
The Great Illumination Mantra says:

“Oṃ mṛgā-ma-vihārādhiṣṭhāna kaṃ maṃ truṃ kha hūṃ traṃ. Furthermore, the ten powers (daśabala) are: the power of knowing what is possible and impossible; the power of knowing the ripening of karma; the power of knowing the various elements; the power of knowing the faculties of oneself and others; the power of knowing the various inclinations and understandings; the power of knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering; the power of knowing defilement and purification; the power of recollecting past lives; the power of the five supernormal knowledges; and the power of the exhaustion of the outflows.
These ten powers are the nature of the equal and excellent arising of all Tathāgatas; this is called the teaching on the Prajñāpāramitā of the equality of the ten powers.
The Great Illumination says:

"Oṃ (1) naśamalamate (2) śvāṅ. Furthermore, regarding the four fearlessnesses: the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having fully realized such dharmas as to have attained perfect enlightenment and possessing all-knowledge, attains fearlessness within the great assembly of all worlds—including devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas;

he observes with equanimity, attaining the practice of great peace and happiness, attaining courageous conduct, and turning the wheel of the true Dharma, which is not turned by any worldly dharmas. Moreover, the Tathāgata, having fully realized such dharmas and exhausted all outflows (āsravas), attains fearlessness.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata teaches that all defiled phenomena obstruct the Noble Path; he speaks with equanimity regarding this teaching and attains fearlessness.
Moreover, the Tathāgata declares that by practicing all correct conducts one can exhaust all suffering; he speaks with equanimity regarding this teaching and attains fearlessness.

These four dharmas are all spoken according to reality; that which is correct, central, and righteous is precisely fearlessness. Abiding equanimously in all phenomena as having the characteristic of being like an illusion, one is free from the nature of "I" and "mine. This is called the teaching of the fearless and equal *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Great Illumination says:

"Oṃ (1) Vaiśāradya-samata-prāpta (2) ā (3) ā (4) aṃ (5) aḥ (6). Furthermore, there are the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), namely: the analytical knowledge of expression, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of meaning, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence.
These four dharmas abide in the state of equality; this is called the Prajñāpāramitā teaching on the unimpeded analytical knowledge of the illusory nature of all phenomena.
The Great Mantra says:

"Oṃ pratisthāna svāhā hūṃ. Furthermore, there are the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), namely: the Tathāgata’s body is without fault, his speech is without fault, and his mind is without fault; he has no lack of concentration, no divergent thoughts, and no equanimity lacking discernment; his aspiration does not diminish, his diligence does not diminish, his mindfulness does not diminish, his wisdom does not diminish, his liberation does not diminish, and his knowledge and vision of liberation does not diminish; he possesses unimpeded and unattached knowledge and vision regarding the turning of vows in the past, unimpeded and unattached knowledge and vision regarding the turning of vows in the future, and unimpeded and unattached knowledge and vision regarding the turning of vows in the present; his physical actions follow the course of wisdom, his verbal actions follow the course of wisdom, and his mental actions follow the course of wisdom.

Regarding these eighteen dharmas, the Tathāgata at all times and in all places dwells perfectly and equanimously; thus he enters into the great wisdom that is pure through the emptiness of all phenomena. This is called the teaching of the uncommon dharma of the equality of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Great Illuminator said:

“Oṃ āvini-gabuddhadharma-samādhi ā vīra hūṃ khaṃ. At that time, all the Tathāgatas who had come from the ten directions, having heard the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, proclaim these secret dharmic phrases, all together praised him by reciting this verse:
“Excellent is the unsurpassed bodhicitta, The supreme sovereignty of all Tathāgatas!”
Excellent is the supreme Dharma of all Buddhas; this is the very name of samādhi.
Excellent is the vast wisdom of Vajra; it is well-established in the firm and solid Vajra-mind.
Excellent are the immeasurable gateways of all dharmas; they are well-established in the pure ultimate truth.
"Thus these secret phrases have been well spoken; all Tathāgatas are born from them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, rejoiced and took refuge in all Tathāgatas, and likewise praised them with a verse, saying:
"I take refuge in and pay homage to all Tathāgatas, The Great Dharma-body, pure in both self and others."
I first take refuge in the secret mantra, the powerful Vajra of firm wisdom.
The ultimate nature of all phenomena is quiescent; abiding in the gateway of the vajra-dharmatā, you have attained the perfected state of the Mahāyāna.
I take refuge in the Great Compassionate Maheśvara.
Primordially pure and greatly fearless, supreme, most excellent, and foremost;
I pay homage with faith to all the Sugatas and the letters of the supreme True Dharma.
Through the gates of the True Dharma thus proclaimed, I universally make offerings to all Buddhas.
A Portion from the Teaching on the Perfection of Wisdom Adorned with the Vajra Realm, Spoken by the Buddha.
